notice: The rule layer is declarative. Rules are validated and machine-readable, but no engine evaluates them against a design problem in v0.1.

derived_from_details.statement: Mott states that sliding motion between a standard parallel key and the mating element should not be permitted, whereas a spline surface is often hardened to resist wear and to facilitate use in applications where axial motion of the mating element is desired.

effect.rationale: Mott states that sliding motion between a standard parallel key and the mating element should not be permitted.

rules.statement: If the required function is transmission of torque between shaft and hub and the operating context requires the mounted element to move axially while torque is transmitted, exclude the plain parallel key connection.
rules.title: Exclude a plain parallel key where the hub must slide under torque

derived_from_details.statement: Shigley states that one feature of a spline is that it can be made with a reasonably loose slip fit to allow large axial motion between shaft and component while still transmitting torque, which is useful for connecting shafts where relative motion is common, such as a tractor power take-off.

Mott states that the SAE spline permanent fit A is used when the mating part is not to be moved after installation, fit B when the mating part will be moved along the shaft without a torque load, and fit C when the mating part must be moved under load; the spline depth h and minor diameter d differ between the fits.

effect.rationale: Shigley states that a spline can be made with a reasonably loose slip fit to allow large axial motion while still transmitting torque. Mott's SAE fit classes distinguish permanent installation (A), movement without torque (B) and movement under load (C).
effect.required_feature: a fit class permitting movement under load

rules.statement: If the required function is transmission of torque between shaft and hub and the context requires axial motion under torque, admit spline connections, provided the spline is specified with a fit that permits sliding.
rules.title: Admit splines where the hub must slide under torque

derived_from_details.statement: Shigley states that excessive safety factors should be avoided in key design, since in an overload situation it is desirable for the key to fail rather than more costly components.

Mott states that the diameter of a pin is sometimes purposely made small to ensure that the pin will break if a moderate overload is encountered, in order to protect critical parts of a mechanism, and that such a pin is called a shear pin.

effect.rationale: Shigley states it is desirable in an overload situation for the key to fail rather than more costly components, and Mott describes the shear pin as a member deliberately sized to break on overload. Replacing a sacrificial member with a friction joint removes that behaviour.

rules.notes: The rule flags rather than excludes: a friction joint can slip rather than break, which is itself a form of overload response. Whether slipping is acceptable is a design judgement the sources do not settle.
rules.statement: If a requirement of kind overload protection is present, flag every alternative whose torque transfer is purely frictional, because such a connection has no member intended to fail first.
rules.title: Flag friction-based connections when overload protection is required

derived_from_details.statement: Mott states that fatigue failures frequently occur within areas of stress concentration such as keyways or grooves in shafts, steps in the size of a cross section, notches and other geometric discontinuities, and that even surface roughness or accidental nicks can initiate cracks.

Shigley states that press and shrink fits for securing hubs to shafts are used both for torque transfer and for preserving axial location, and that the resulting stress-concentration factor is usually quite small.

effect.rationale: Mott lists keyways in shafts among the stress concentrations at which fatigue failures frequently occur; Shigley states that the stress-concentration factor resulting from a press or shrink fit is usually quite small.

rules.notes: A press fit is not free of stress concentration: Shigley records a raiser in the shaft bending stress near the hub ends, with first estimates typically not greater than 2. The preference is comparative, not absolute.
rules.statement: If shaft fatigue life at the connection is a governing requirement, prefer connections that do not require a keyseat in the shaft.
rules.title: Prefer alternatives without a keyseat when shaft fatigue governs

derived_from_details.statement: Shigley states that for cases of low torque transmission various means of transmitting torque are available, including pins, setscrews in hubs, tapered fits and press fits.

effect.rationale: Shigley introduces these four as the means available for cases of low torque transmission.

rules.not_executable_because: The source gives no numeric boundary for 'low torque', and none may be introduced. The rule is advisory until an external standard, company specification or engineering review supplies a threshold.
rules.statement: Treat pins, setscrews in hubs, tapered fits and press fits as candidates for cases of low torque transmission.
rules.title: Restrict setscrew, pin, tapered-fit and press-fit connections to low torque

derived_from_details.statement: Mott states that the involute spline form is preferred because it provides self-centering of the mating element and because it can be machined with standard hobs used to cut gear teeth.

effect.rationale: Mott states the involute form is preferred because it self-centres the mating element and can be machined with standard gear hobs.

rules.notes: Mott states this preference without attaching an operating context, so the rule carries context_unspecified rather than an invented one.
rules.statement: Where a spline is selected, prefer the involute form.
rules.title: Prefer the involute spline form over the straight-sided form

derived_from_details.statement: Shigley states that tapered roller bearings combine the advantages of ball and straight roller bearings, since they can take radial or thrust loads or any combination of the two, and additionally have the high load-carrying capacity of straight roller bearings.

effect.rationale: Shigley describes tapered roller bearings as taking radial or thrust loads or any combination of the two, distinguishing them from families described only in radial terms.

rules.notes: Marked analyst-authored because the exclusion rests on the function assignments in this ontology, not on a cited statement that particular families cannot take thrust.
rules.statement: If the support must carry a thrust load, exclude alternatives that do not perform the carry-thrust-load function.
rules.title: Require a thrust-capable support where thrust load is present

derived_from_details.statement: Mott states that the tabulated bearing data in the book are similar to those in manufacturers' catalogues, and that it is essential that published data from specific manufacturers be used in any real application.

Shigley states that each manufacturer chooses a specific rating life for which load ratings are reported, that the most commonly used rating life is 10^6 revolutions, and that at least one well-known manufacturer instead rates bearings at 3000 hours at 500 rev/min, equal to 90 million revolutions.

effect.rationale: Mott states it is essential that published data from specific manufacturers be used in any real application; Shigley notes each manufacturer chooses its own rating-life basis.

rules.statement: Any bearing selection intended for a real application must be closed against the specific manufacturer's published data, not against textbook tables.
rules.title: Require manufacturer data for any real bearing selection

rules.notes: Encodes the definition of FunctionalAlternative from ontology/core/substitution.ttl. Not terminal: later rules may strengthen or weaken the verdict on evidence about context and interfaces.
rules.statement: If a candidate and a baseline both perform the preserved function, and nothing further is known, the verdict is FunctionalAlternative. This is the ceiling that co-function alone can justify.
rules.title: A shared function establishes at most a functional alternative

rules.statement: If the candidate does not perform the preserved function in the stated context, or its interface is incompatible and no modification is offered, the verdict is NotAnAlternative.
rules.title: A candidate that cannot deliver the preserved function is not an alternative

derived_from_details.statement: Mott states that sliding motion between a standard parallel key and the mating element should not be permitted, whereas a spline surface is often hardened to resist wear and to facilitate use in applications where axial motion of the mating element is desired.

rules.notes: Instantiated by SA-006: a parallel key violates the axial-motion requirement in a context that demands sliding under torque, so it is not an alternative there, even though it is one elsewhere.
rules.statement: If the candidate violates a requirement that is applicable in the stated context, and that requirement expresses the reason the baseline was chosen, the verdict is NotAnAlternative in that context.
rules.title: A violated requirement in the stated context defeats substitution

effect.requires: at least one condition or one required modification must be recorded

rules.notes: The `requires` clause is not decoration; SHACL enforces it, so a ConditionallySubstitutable verdict with no condition and no modification fails validation.
rules.statement: If the candidate preserves the function but only under stated conditions, or only after stated design modifications, the verdict is ConditionallySubstitutable.
rules.title: Named conditions or modifications yield a conditional verdict

rules.notes: No assessment in v0.1 reaches this verdict. That is a finding, not a gap: every pair examined in the pilot requires at least a change of shaft or hub feature, so none is a drop-in replacement.
prohibitions: MUST NOT be concluded from a shared function alone.
MUST NOT be concluded from the absence of contrary evidence.
rules.statement: A verdict of DirectlySubstitutable may be reached only when the interface is identical, no applicable requirement is violated, no design modification is required, and the context conditions are unchanged.
rules.title: Direct substitutability requires positive interface and requirement evidence

rules.notes: Instantiated by SA-001, where the spline is preferred because the context makes axial motion a requirement. Change the requirement set and the preference disappears: Shigley calls splines usually unnecessary for simple torque transmission.
rules.statement: A verdict of PreferredAlternative may be reached only when the candidate is at least conditionally substitutable AND outperforms the baseline on a requirement that is applicable in the stated context. The preference is relative to that requirement set and is not a general ranking.
rules.title: Preference requires a stated requirement set

derived_from_details.statement: Shigley states that for cases of low torque transmission various means of transmitting torque are available, including pins, setscrews in hubs, tapered fits and press fits.
Shigley states that splines are typically used to transfer high torques.

rules.notes: Instantiated by SA-003, whose applicability depends on 'low torque transmission'. The human-readable conditional verdict is retained; only automated evaluation degrades to InsufficientEvidence.
rules.statement: If the applicability of a substitution turns on a qualitative threshold that no cited source quantifies, the verdict for automated evaluation is InsufficientEvidence, regardless of how well the alternatives otherwise match.
rules.title: An unfixable threshold yields insufficient evidence

derived_from_details.statement: Mott gives the load/life exponent k as 3.00 for ball bearings and 3.33 for roller bearings.
Shigley states that regression of many tests on the load-life relation F L^(1/a) = constant gives a = 3 for ball bearings and a = 10/3 for roller bearings, both cylindrical and tapered.

rules.notes: Both books give 3 for ball bearings and 3.33 or 10/3 for roller bearings. They also warn that the exponent is meaningless without the rating-life basis it was fitted against, which differs between manufacturers.
rules.statement: When the candidate and the baseline belong to bearing families with different load-life exponents, any life or capacity comparison must be recomputed with the candidate's exponent. Carrying the baseline's result across is invalid.
rules.title: Substituting across a load-life exponent boundary invalidates the baseline life calculation

derived_from_details.statement: Mott states that the diameter of a pin is sometimes purposely made small to ensure that the pin will break if a moderate overload is encountered, in order to protect critical parts of a mechanism, and that such a pin is called a shear pin.
Shigley states that excessive safety factors should be avoided in key design, since in an overload situation it is desirable for the key to fail rather than more costly components.

effect.scope: where overload protection is a stated requirement

rules.notes: Guards against the common error of treating a stronger connection as strictly better. Mott's shear pin and Shigley's fusible key are both intended to fail.
rules.statement: If the baseline performs the limit-transmitted-torque function and the candidate does not, the substitution is not function-preserving even when torque capacity is equal or greater.
rules.title: Removing a sacrificial member is a loss of function, not a neutral change

acceptance.statement: Actual stress must not exceed the design stress obtained by dividing the relevant strength by the design factor. Bearing failure is assessed against whichever of key, shaft keyseat or hub keyseat has the lowest compressive yield strength.

derived_from_details.statement: Mott states that there are two basic modes of potential failure for keys transmitting power: shear across the shaft/hub interface, and compression failure due to the bearing action between the sides of the key and the shaft or hub material.

Mott sets the shearing stress equal to a design stress in shear based on the maximum shear stress theory of failure, tau_d = 0.5 s_y / N, and obtains the minimum required key length for shear as L_min = 2T / (tau_d D W), where T is torque, D the shaft diameter and W the key width.

Mott states that failure in bearing relates to the compressive stress on the side of the key, the shaft keyseat or the hub keyseat; the compression area is the same for each, so failure occurs on the surface with the lowest compressive yield strength.

Mott states that where a rectangular key is used, or where the shaft or hub has lower strength than the key, the minimum lengths for bearing and for shear must both be computed and the larger governs; the result must be checked against the available hub length.

Shigley states that failure of a key can be by direct shear or by bearing stress, that the shaft diameter determines standard sizes for key width, height and depth, and that the designer chooses the key length to carry the torsional load.

rules.statement: Any parallel key connection must be checked for direct shear and for bearing (compressive) stress. Where the two give different required lengths, the larger governs.
rules.title: A key connection requires both a shear check and a bearing check

acceptance.statement: Numeric stress-concentration factors for an end-milled keyseat are cited by Shigley from an external stress-concentration reference. Those numbers are NOT reproduced here: they fall in mathematics-font runs that this PDF's text layer mis-maps, and they originate outside the book.

derived_from_details.statement: Mott states that fatigue failures frequently occur within areas of stress concentration such as keyways or grooves in shafts, steps in the size of a cross section, notches and other geometric discontinuities, and that even surface roughness or accidental nicks can initiate cracks.
Shigley states that it is necessary to know where shaft discontinuities such as keyways, holes and splines will be, in order to determine the critical locations for analysis.

Shigley cites published stress-concentration charts giving factors for an end-milled keyseat as a function of the ratio of the groove-bottom radius to the shaft diameter, with separate values for bending and for torsion, and with a further distinction for torsion with the key in place.
Shigley states that stress-concentration factors for splines are greatest where the spline ends and blends into the shaft, but are generally quite moderate.

rules.statement: Where a keyseat, transverse hole or spline run-out is present in a shaft under cyclic loading, the stress concentration at that feature must be assessed as part of the shaft fatigue check.
rules.title: A keyed or splined shaft requires a stress-concentration assessment

acceptance.statement: The form of the capacity equation is given, but the cited sections do not fix a coefficient of friction for the joint. The capacity therefore cannot be closed from these two books alone.

derived_from_details.statement: Shigley states that the torque an interference fit can transmit is estimated by a simple friction analysis at the interface, the friction force being the product of the coefficient of friction and the normal force, giving a torque capacity T = (pi/2) f p l d^2, where f is the coefficient of friction, p the interface pressure, l the hub length and d the nominal shaft diameter.

Shigley states that the minimum interference should be used to determine the minimum pressure, which in turn bounds the maximum torque the joint should be designed to transmit without slipping; the maximum interference is used instead to check for excessive stress.

Shigley states that a press fit produces a stress-concentration effect in the shaft bending stress near the ends of the hub, due to the sudden change from compressed to uncompressed material, that hub geometry makes generalised values difficult to report, and that for first estimates values are typically not greater than 2.

open_parameters.name: coefficient of friction at the shaft/hub interface
open_parameters.status: not specified by either cited source

rules.statement: An interference-fit connection must be evaluated at both interference extremes: the maximum interference to check for excessive stress, and the minimum interference to bound the torque the joint may be designed to transmit without slipping.
rules.title: An interference fit requires a pressure calculation at both tolerance extremes

acceptance.statement: Mott recommends testing but defines no procedure: no instrumentation, no load sequence, no cycle count and no pass criterion. The ontology records the recommendation and the three gaps, and supplies none of them.

derived_from_details.statement: Mott introduces methods of attaching power-transmitting elements to shafts without keys or splines, noting that in most cases these designs have not been standardised and that analysis of individual cases considering the forces and manner of loading is necessary.
Mott states that if a satisfactory analysis of a keyless attachment method is not possible, testing of the assembly is recommended.

rules.statement: Where a shaft/hub attachment method is not standardised and a satisfactory analysis is not possible, testing of the assembly is recommended.
rules.title: A non-standardised keyless connection requires testing that neither book defines

acceptance.statement: The computed required basic dynamic load rating must not exceed the catalogue rating of the selected bearing, and the applied static load must not exceed the basic static load rating.

derived_from_details.statement: Mott states the relationship between load P and life L for rolling contact bearings as L2 / L1 = (P1 / P2)^k.

Mott states that the basic static load rating C_o is the load the bearing can withstand without permanent deformation of any component; exceeding it most probably indents a race, a failure referred to as brinelling, after which operation would be noisy and progressive failure would follow.

Mott states that where manufacturer load data are reported for one million revolutions, the design life is L_d = (C / P_d)^k times 10^6 and the required basic dynamic load rating is C = P_d (L_d / 10^6)^(1/k), with design revolutions obtained from hours of operation and shaft speed.

Mott states that the tabulated bearing data in the book are similar to those in manufacturers' catalogues, and that it is essential that published data from specific manufacturers be used in any real application.

Shigley states that the rating life, a term sanctioned by the ABMA and used by most manufacturers, is the number of revolutions or hours at constant speed that 90 percent of a group of nominally identical bearings will achieve or exceed before the failure criterion develops; it is the 10th percentile of the revolutions-to-failure distribution.

Shigley states that each manufacturer chooses a specific rating life for which load ratings are reported, that the most commonly used rating life is 10^6 revolutions, and that at least one well-known manufacturer instead rates bearings at 3000 hours at 500 rev/min, equal to 90 million revolutions.
Shigley states that regression of many tests on the load-life relation F L^(1/a) = constant gives a = 3 for ball bearings and a = 10/3 for roller bearings, both cylindrical and tapered.

Shigley states that a catalog load rating, denoted C10, is the radial load that causes 10 percent of a group of bearings to fail at the manufacturer's rating life, and is often called the Basic Dynamic Load Rating when the rating life is one million revolutions.

preconditions.statement: The catalogue rating-life basis must be established before the load-life equation is applied. One million revolutions is the most common basis but is not universal.
The correct exponent for the bearing family must be used: 3 for ball bearings, 3.33 or 10/3 for roller bearings.

rules.statement: A rolling-contact bearing selection must be checked for rating life under the operating load and, separately, against the basic static load rating for the largest load applied while stationary or slow-moving.
rules.title: A rolling bearing requires both a rating-life and a static-rating check

acceptance.statement: Shigley gives typical factors of safety of 1.5 to 2.0 for static loads and 4 to 8 for various dynamic loads, applied to tabulated holding power for both axial and tangential directions.

derived_from_details.statement: Shigley states that typical factors of safety applied to tabulated setscrew holding power are 1.5 to 2.0 for static loads and 4 to 8 for various dynamic loads, the tabulated values applying to both axial and tangential holding power.

rules.notes: The tabulated holding-power values themselves are not reproduced in this ontology; the rule cites their location.
rules.statement: A setscrew connection is checked by comparing the applied axial or tangential load against tabulated holding power, derated by a factor of safety chosen for the loading type.
rules.title: A setscrew connection is verified against tabulated holding power with a load-type factor

acceptance.statement: Capacity is based on an assumed limit of 1000 psi bearing stress on the sides of the splines.

derived_from_details.statement: Mott states that the torque capacity for SAE straight-sided splines is based on a limit of 1000 psi bearing stress on the sides of the splines, from which T = 1000 N R h is derived, where N is the number of splines, R the mean radius and h the spline depth. The torque capacity is per inch of spline length.

rules.notes: Recorded as a verification rule rather than a note because silently applying this formula in SI, or forgetting the per-inch basis, is a plausible and consequential error.
rules.statement: Mott's SAE straight-sided spline torque capacity is stated in inch units with torque in pound-inches, and is a capacity PER INCH of engaged spline length. It must be multiplied by the engaged length and must not be used in SI without conversion.
rules.title: A spline capacity calculation must respect its unit system and length basis
unit_constraints: Dimensions in inches; torque in pound-inches.
Result is per inch of spline length.
The equation is not dimensionally general and does not carry over to SI unchanged.
